questions.q: How does table partitioning's use of "PARTITION BY"-style concepts relate to the OVER (PARTITION BY ...) window function from T-SQL Development?
options: They are unrelated despite sharing a word — table partitioning is a physical storage decision, while the window function clause only groups rows for a calculation
They are the exact same feature with two different names
Table partitioning is just a faster version of the window function
T-SQL Development already fully taught table partitioning under a different name
questions.explain: Table partitioning splits a table's physical storage by a column's value; the window-function PARTITION BY only affects how a calculation groups rows, with no effect on storage.

questions.q: What are the two objects you create before building a partitioned table, and what does each one do?
options: A partition FUNCTION (defines the boundary values) and a partition SCHEME (maps each range onto a filegroup)
A partition INDEX and a partition VIEW
A partition TRIGGER and a partition PROCEDURE
Only a single CREATE PARTITION statement is needed — nothing else
questions.explain: CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION defines where the boundaries fall; CREATE PARTITION SCHEME maps each resulting range onto a filegroup. The table is then created on the scheme.

questions.q: What is the primary, most common reason a DBA partitions a very large table, according to this lesson?
options: Maintenance operations like index rebuilds can target one partition instead of the entire table
It's required before a table can hold more than 1,000 rows
It automatically encrypts the table's data
It removes the need for indexes entirely
questions.explain: Rebuilding one fragmented partition instead of an entire multi-hundred-million-row table is the main driver; query performance is a secondary bonus.

questions.q: What is "partition elimination," and when does it help a query?
options: The optimizer skips partitions it knows can't contain matching rows, when a query filters on the partitioning column
It permanently deletes old partitions from the table
It removes all indexes from a partition
It merges every partition back into a single unpartitioned table
questions.explain: When a query's WHERE clause filters on the partitioning column, the optimizer can skip scanning partitions that are guaranteed not to match — a query-performance bonus on top of the maintenance win.

questions.q: In the example CREATE TABLE ... ON PS_OrderDateRange (OrderDate), what determines which partition a given row lands in?
options: The value in that row's OrderDate column, compared against the partition function's boundary values
The order in which rows were inserted, regardless of column values
A random assignment made by SQL Server at insert time
The row's OrderID value only
questions.explain: The table is partitioned on the OrderDate column; each row's OrderDate value is checked against the partition function's boundaries to decide which partition it belongs to.
